source.text: נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּ֣ר מַלְכָּ֗א עֲבַד֙ צְלֵ֣ם דִּֽי־דְהַ֔ב רוּמֵהּ֙ אַמִּ֣ין שִׁתִּ֔ין פְּתָיֵ֖הּ אַמִּ֣ין שִׁ֑ת אֲקִימֵהּ֙ בְּבִקְעַ֣ת דּוּרָ֔א בִּמְדִינַ֖ת בָּבֶֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold; its height [was] cubits sixty, its width cubits six; he set it up on [the] plain of Dura in [the] province of Babylon.

en.L: Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold; its height [was] sixty cubits, its breadth six cubits. He erected it on the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon.
en.B: King Nebuchadnezzar made a gold statue {{units:about 90 feet|sixty cubits}} high and {{units:about 9 feet|six cubits}} wide, and he had it set up on the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon.
en.R: King Nebuchadnezzar had a gold statue made. It was {{units:about 90 feet|sixty cubits}} tall and {{units:about 9 feet|six cubits}} wide. He had it placed on the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon.

decisions.choice: an image of gold: a statue covered with gold
alternatives: a statue of the king himself
decisions.reason: A statue of this size would hardly have been solid gold; like the idols the prophets mock, it was probably made of wood or another material overlaid with gold (Isaiah 40:19; Jeremiah 10:3-4). The text does not say whom it represented: a god of Babylon, or the king himself, or his rule. The king's charge in verses 12, 14 and 18, that the Jews do not serve his gods and do not bow to the image, keeps the two side by side. The image recalls the statue of the king's dream, whose head of gold was Nebuchadnezzar (2:38).

decisions.choice: sixty cubits high and six cubits wide
decisions.reason: A cubit was about 18 inches, so the image was about 90 feet high and 9 feet wide, much taller than it was broad. It may have stood on a high base, or been a pillar with a figure on top. Babylon counted in sixties, which may lie behind the numbers.

decisions.choice: the plain of Dura: a place in the province of Babylon
decisions.reason: Several places near Babylon bore the name Dura, which means "walled place" in Babylonian, and the exact site is not known. A plain gave room for the great crowd of verses 2-3.

decisions.choice: {{units:about 90 feet|sixty cubits}} ... {{units:about 9 feet|six cubits}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the size in modern measures by default, with the cubits as the setting's alternative, reckoned at about 18 inches to the cubit (m2). Literal keeps the cubits.

source.text: וּנְבוּכַדְנֶצַּ֣ר מַלְכָּ֡א שְׁלַ֡ח לְמִכְנַ֣שׁ׀לַֽאֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנַיָּ֡א סִגְנַיָּ֣א וּֽפַחֲוָתָ֡א אֲדַרְגָּזְרַיָּא֩ גְדָ֨בְרַיָּ֤א דְּתָבְרַיָּא֙ תִּפְתָּיֵ֔א וְכֹ֖ל שִׁלְטֹנֵ֣י מְדִֽינָתָ֑א לְמֵתֵא֙ לַחֲנֻכַּ֣ת צַלְמָ֔א דִּ֥י הֲקֵ֖ים נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּ֥ר מַלְכָּֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: And Nebuchadnezzar the king sent to gather the satraps, the prefects and the governors, the counselors, the treasurers, the judges, the magistrates, and all [the] authorities of the provinces to come to the dedication of the image which had set up Nebuchadnezzar the king.

en.L: And Nebuchadnezzar the king sent to gather the satraps, the prefects and the governors, the counselors, the treasurers, the judges, the magistrates, and all the authorities of the provinces, to come to the dedication of the image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up.
en.B: Then King Nebuchadnezzar sent word to gather the satraps, the prefects, the governors, the counselors, the treasurers, the judges, the magistrates and all the officials of the provinces to come to the dedication of the statue that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.
en.R: Then King Nebuchadnezzar sent for the regional governors, the prefects, the governors, the advisers, the treasurers, the judges, the magistrates and all the other officials of the provinces. He wanted them to come to the dedication of the statue he had set up.

decisions.choice: the satraps, the prefects, the governors ...: every rank of the empire's officials
decisions.reason: The list names the officials of the empire from the highest down. The satraps ruled the great regions of the empire (the title is Persian, and Esther and Ezra use it of the Persian empire); the prefects and governors ruled provinces and districts; the counselors, treasurers, judges and magistrates had charge of advice, money and law. Several of the titles are Persian words, and the exact duties of some are not certain. The list is repeated in verse 3, with something of a mocking tone: the whole machine of the empire is gathered to bow at once.

decisions.choice: the dedication of the image: the ceremony that set it apart for use
decisions.reason: The same word is used of the dedication of the altar, the temple and Jerusalem's wall (Numbers 7:10; Ezra 6:16; Nehemiah 12:27). The king's ceremony is a rival to the worship of Israel's God.

decisions.choice: satraps (L, B); regional governors (R)
decisions.reason: The terms for Daniel set "satraps" at Literal and Balanced, and "regional governors" at Readable, as in Esther and Ezra. The rest of the list is kept at every level, since its length is part of the story; Readable gives plain titles such as "advisers".

source.text: בֵּאדַ֡יִן מִֽתְכַּנְּשִׁ֡ין אֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנַיָּ֡א סִגְנַיָּ֣א וּֽפַחֲוָתָ֡א אֲדַרְגָּזְרַיָּ֣א גְדָבְרַיָּא֩ דְּתָ֨בְרַיָּ֜א תִּפְתָּיֵ֗א וְכֹל֙ שִׁלְטֹנֵ֣י מְדִֽינָתָ֔א לַחֲנֻכַּ֣ת צַלְמָ֔א דִּ֥י הֲקֵ֖ים נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּ֣ר מַלְכָּ֑א וְקָֽיְמִין֙ לָקֳבֵ֣ל צַלְמָ֔א דִּ֥י הֲקֵ֖ים נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: Then were gathered the satraps, the prefects and the governors, the counselors, the treasurers, the judges, the magistrates, and all [the] authorities of the provinces, for the dedication of the image which had set up Nebuchadnezzar the king; and [they were] standing before the image which had set up Nebuchadnezzar.

en.L: Then the satraps, the prefects and the governors, the counselors, the treasurers, the judges, the magistrates, and all the authorities of the provinces were gathered for the dedication of the image which Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up; and they were standing before the image which Nebuchadnezzar had set up.
en.B: So the satraps, the prefects, the governors, the counselors, the treasurers, the judges, the magistrates and all the officials of the provinces gathered for the dedication of the statue King Nebuchadnezzar had set up. They stood in front of the statue Nebuchadnezzar had set up.
en.R: So the regional governors, the prefects, the governors, the advisers, the treasurers, the judges, the magistrates and all the other officials of the provinces came together for the dedication of the statue. They stood in front of the statue that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.

decisions.choice: the image that Nebuchadnezzar had set up: a phrase repeated through the chapter
decisions.reason: The words "the image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up" return again and again (verses 2, 3, 5, 7, 12, 14, 18). The repetition shows how much the king's own pride is bound up in the image.

decisions.choice: came together for the dedication of the statue (R)
decisions.reason: Readable does not repeat "that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up" twice in one verse, though the repetition is part of the Aramaic style (m1); Literal and Balanced keep it.

source.text: וְכָרוֹזָ֖א קָרֵ֣א בְחָ֑יִל לְכ֤וֹן אָֽמְרִין֙ עַֽמְמַיָּ֔א אֻמַּיָּ֖א וְלִשָּׁנַיָּֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: And the herald [was] proclaiming with strength: To you [it is] said, O peoples, nations and languages:

en.L: And the herald proclaimed with strength, "To you it is commanded, O peoples, nations and languages:
en.B: Then the herald called out loudly, "Peoples, nations and people of every language, this is the command to you:
en.R: Then a man with a loud voice announced, "People of every nation and language, listen to this command!

decisions.choice: peoples, nations and languages: people of every race and tongue
decisions.reason: This phrase for all the peoples of the empire is common in Daniel (3:7, 29, 31; 5:19; 6:26; 7:14). "Languages" stands for the people who speak them. In 7:14 the same three words describe the peoples who will serve the one like a son of man.

decisions.choice: the herald: the officer who proclaimed the king's orders aloud
decisions.reason: The word is used only here in the Old Testament. Royal orders were read out in public by a herald, so that no one could plead ignorance.

decisions.choice: people of every language (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Languages" stands for the people who speak them (m1); Balanced and Readable say so. The command runs on into verse 5, so the verse ends with a colon or an exclamation.

source.text: בְּעִדָּנָ֡א דִּֽי־תִשְׁמְע֡וּן קָ֣ל קַרְנָ֣א מַ֠שְׁרוֹקִיתָא קַתְר֨וֹס סַבְּכָ֤א פְּסַנְתֵּרִין֙ סוּמְפֹּ֣נְיָ֔ה וְכֹ֖ל זְנֵ֣י זְמָרָ֑א תִּפְּל֤וּן וְתִסְגְּדוּן֙ לְצֶ֣לֶם דַּהֲבָ֔א דִּ֥י הֲקֵ֖ים נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּ֥ר מַלְכָּֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: At the time that you hear [the] sound of the horn, the pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe, and all kinds of music, you will fall down and pay homage to [the] image of gold which has set up Nebuchadnezzar the king.

en.L: At the time you hear the sound of the horn, the pipe, the lyre, the trigon, the harp, the bagpipe, and every kind of music, you shall fall down and worship the image of gold that Nebuchadnezzar the king has set up.
en.B: As soon as you hear the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe and every kind of music, you must fall down and worship the gold statue that King Nebuchadnezzar has set up.
en.R: When you hear the sound of the horns, flutes, lyres, zithers, harps, bagpipes and all the other instruments, you must bow down to the ground and worship the gold statue that King Nebuchadnezzar has set up.

decisions.choice: the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe: the instruments of the royal band
alternatives: the last word as a double pipe or a drum
decisions.reason: The names of the instruments are uncertain. The horn was an animal horn; the pipe was a wind instrument; the lyre, trigon and harp were stringed instruments, the trigon a small triangular harp. The last word, *sumponyah*, may be a bagpipe, a double pipe or a drum, or it may mean "in concert" (all playing together). Three of the names are Greek words (lyre, harp and the last), which shows that such instruments, or their names, had reached the East. The list returns four times (verses 5, 7, 10, 15) and is part of the story's style.

decisions.choice: fall down and worship: bow to the ground in worship
decisions.reason: The second verb means to bow down in homage, the gesture used before a king or a god (2:46). Here, before an image at its dedication, it is an act of worship, and that is why the three Jews refuse (verse 18; Exodus 20:4-5).

decisions.choice: horns, flutes, lyres, zithers, harps, bagpipes (R)
decisions.reason: Readable gives the instruments in plural and calls the trigon a zither, a stringed instrument young readers may know. It keeps the list, which is part of the story's repetition.

source.text: וּמַן־דִּי־לָ֥א יִפֵּ֖ל וְיִסְגֻּ֑ד בַּהּ־שַׁעֲתָ֣א יִתְרְמֵ֔א לְגֽוֹא־אַתּ֥וּן נוּרָ֖א יָקִֽדְתָּֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: And whoever not falls down and pays homage, at that moment he will be thrown into [the] midst of [the] furnace of the fire burning.

en.L: And whoever does not fall down and worship, at that moment will be thrown into the midst of a furnace of burning fire."
en.B: Anyone who does not fall down and worship will immediately be thrown into a blazing furnace."
en.R: Anyone who does not bow down and worship will be thrown at once into a very hot furnace."

decisions.choice: a furnace of burning fire: a large kiln
decisions.reason: This was probably a large kiln for firing bricks or smelting metal, with an opening at the top for fuel and a door at the side through which those inside could be seen (verses 25-26). Burning as a punishment is known from Babylon (Jeremiah 29:22).

decisions.choice: at that moment: immediately
decisions.reason: The word means "the hour" or "the moment" and stresses that punishment would be immediate.

decisions.choice: a blazing furnace (B); a very hot furnace (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Aramaic "a furnace of burning fire", which recurs through the chapter; Balanced and Readable use shorter phrases with the same meaning.

source.text: כָּל־קֳבֵ֣ל דְּנָ֡ה בֵּהּ־זִמְנָ֡א כְּדִ֣י שָֽׁמְעִ֣ין כָּֽל־עַמְמַיָּ֡א קָ֣ל קַרְנָא֩ מַשְׁר֨וֹקִיתָ֜א קַתְר֤וֹס שַׂבְּכָא֙ פְּסַנְטֵרִ֔ין וְכֹ֖ל זְנֵ֣י זְמָרָ֑א נָֽפְלִ֨ין כָּֽל־עַֽמְמַיָּ֜א אֻמַיָּ֣א וְלִשָּׁנַיָּ֗א סָֽגְדִין֙ לְצֶ֣לֶם דַּהֲבָ֔א דִּ֥י הֲקֵ֖ים נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּ֥ר מַלְכָּֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: Because of this, at the time when all the peoples heard [the] sound of the horn, the pipe, lyre, trigon, harp and all kinds of music, falling down all the peoples, nations and languages [were] paying homage to [the] image of gold which had set up Nebuchadnezzar the king.

en.L: Therefore at that time, as soon as all the peoples heard the sound of the horn, the pipe, the lyre, the trigon, the harp and every kind of music, all the peoples, nations and languages fell down [and] worshiped the image of gold that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up.
en.B: So as soon as all the peoples heard the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp and every kind of music, all the peoples, nations and people of every language fell down and worshiped the gold statue that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.
en.R: So when everyone heard the sound of the horns, flutes, lyres, zithers, harps and all the other instruments, people of every nation and language bowed down and worshiped the gold statue King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.

decisions.choice: the list of instruments: the bagpipe is not named here
alternatives: the full list, as in verse 5
decisions.reason: Here the list leaves out the last instrument of verse 5, though it returns in verses 10 and 15. Some ancient manuscripts and versions add it. The difference does not change the sense.

decisions.choice: fell down ... worshiped: everyone obeyed at once
decisions.reason: The crowd obeys exactly as ordered, using the very words of the command. The story sets this up so that the refusal of the three stands out.

decisions.choice: fell down [and] worshiped (L)
decisions.reason: The two Aramaic verbs stand side by side without "and"; Literal supplies it in brackets.

source.text: כָּל־קֳבֵ֤ל דְּנָה֙ בֵּהּ־זִמְנָ֔א קְרִ֖בוּ גֻּבְרִ֣ין כַּשְׂדָּאִ֑ין וַאֲכַ֥לוּ קַרְצֵיה֖וֹן דִּ֥י יְהוּדָיֵֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: Because of this, at that time approached men, Chaldeans, and they ate the pieces of the Jews.

en.L: Therefore at that time certain men, Chaldeans, came forward and ate the pieces of the Jews.
en.B: Then at that time some Chaldeans came forward and brought malicious charges against the Jews.
en.R: At that time some Babylonians came to the king and accused the Jews.

decisions.choice: ate the pieces of the Jews: slandered them, brought malicious accusations
decisions.reason: This is an Aramaic idiom for accusing someone with malice, perhaps from the picture of tearing an enemy to pieces and eating him. It is used again in 6:25 of Daniel's accusers.

decisions.choice: men, Chaldeans: Babylonians, perhaps members of the class of experts
alternatives: members of the class of court experts
decisions.reason: The word can mean Chaldeans as a people or as the class of experts of chapter 2. The contrast here between "Chaldean men" and "the Jews" points to the people, men of Babylonian birth who resented the foreigners set over the province (2:49). Some think that they were experts of the court, rivals of the Jews.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the people from Judah
decisions.reason: "Jew" first meant a person of Judah (Jeremiah 32:12). In exile it became the name for the whole people.

decisions.choice: brought malicious charges (B); accused (R); Babylonians (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the idiom; Balanced and Readable say what it means (m1). Readable takes "Chaldeans" as the people, "Babylonians", as the terms for Daniel set where the word means the people (m2).

source.text: עֲנוֹ֙ וְאָ֣מְרִ֔ין לִנְבוּכַדְנֶצַּ֖ר מַלְכָּ֑א מַלְכָּ֖א לְעָלְמִ֥ין חֱיִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: They answered and saying to Nebuchadnezzar the king: O king, forever live!

en.L: They answered and said to Nebuchadnezzar the king, "O king, live forever!
en.B: They said to King Nebuchadnezzar, "O king, may you live forever!
en.R: They said to King Nebuchadnezzar, "Your Majesty, may you live forever!

decisions.choice: O king, live forever: the greeting of the court
decisions.reason: See 2:4. The accusers begin with the usual courtesy before they make their charge.

decisions.choice: Your Majesty (R)
decisions.reason: As in 2:4, Readable says "Your Majesty" for "O king".

source.text: אַ֣נְתְּ מַלְכָּא֮ שָׂ֣מְתָּ טְּעֵם֒ דִּ֣י כָל־אֱנָ֡שׁ דִּֽי־יִשְׁמַ֡ע קָ֣ל קַרְנָ֣א מַ֠שְׁרֹקִיתָא קַתְר֨וֹס שַׂבְּכָ֤א פְסַנְתֵּרִין֙ וְסוּפֹּ֣נְיָ֔ה וְכֹ֖ל זְנֵ֣י זְמָרָ֑א יִפֵּ֥ל וְיִסְגֻּ֖ד לְצֶ֥לֶם דַּהֲבָֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: You, O king, have made a decree that every man who hears [the] sound of the horn, the pipe, lyre, trigon, harp and bagpipe, and all kinds of music, will fall down and pay homage to [the] image of gold,

en.L: You, O king, have made a decree that every person who hears the sound of the horn, the pipe, the lyre, the trigon, the harp and the bagpipe, and every kind of music, shall fall down and worship the image of gold,
en.B: You, O king, have made a decree: everyone who hears the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe and every kind of music must fall down and worship the gold statue,
en.R: Your Majesty, you gave an order that everyone must bow down and worship the gold statue when they hear the horns, flutes, lyres, zithers, harps, bagpipes and all the other instruments.

decisions.choice: every person who hears: the decree covered everyone
decisions.reason: The accusers remind the king of his own decree in its full form, so that he cannot excuse the Jews. The word for "person" means any human being.

decisions.choice: a comma at the end (L, B)
decisions.reason: The sentence runs on into verse 11, so Literal and Balanced end the verse with a comma; Readable makes it a sentence of its own.

source.text: וּמַן־דִּי־לָ֥א יִפֵּ֖ל וְיִסְגֻּ֑ד יִתְרְמֵ֕א לְגֽוֹא־אַתּ֥וּן נוּרָ֖א יָקִֽדְתָּֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: and whoever not falls down and pays homage will be thrown into [the] midst of [the] furnace of the fire burning.

en.L: and whoever does not fall down and worship shall be thrown into the midst of a furnace of burning fire.
en.B: and that anyone who does not fall down and worship will be thrown into a blazing furnace.
en.R: You said that anyone who does not bow down and worship will be thrown into a very hot furnace.

decisions.choice: whoever does not fall down: the words of the herald in verse 6
decisions.reason: The accusers repeat the threat of verse 6 almost word for word.

decisions.choice: You said that (R)
decisions.reason: Readable starts a new sentence and adds "You said" to make clear that this is still the king's decree.

source.text: אִיתַ֞י גֻּבְרִ֣ין יְהוּדָאיִ֗ן דִּֽי־מַנִּ֤יתָ יָתְהוֹן֙ עַל־עֲבִידַת֙ מְדִינַ֣ת בָּבֶ֔ל שַׁדְרַ֥ךְ מֵישַׁ֖ךְ וַעֲבֵ֣ד נְג֑וֹ גֻּבְרַיָּ֣א אִלֵּ֗ךְ לָא־שָׂ֨מֽוּ עֲלָ֤ךְ מַלְכָּא֙ טְעֵ֔ם לֵֽאלָהָךְ֙ לָ֣א פָלְחִ֔ין וּלְצֶ֧לֶם דַּהֲבָ֛א דִּ֥י הֲקֵ֖ימְתָּ לָ֥א סָגְדִֽין׃ס

records.literal_gloss: There are men, Jews, whom you have appointed over [the] administration of [the] province of Babylon, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego; the men these have not set upon you, O king, regard; your gods not [are they] serving, and to [the] image of gold which you have set up not [are they] paying homage.

en.L: There are certain Jews whom you have appointed over the administration of the province of Babylon: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. These men have paid no regard to you, O king; they do not serve your gods, and they do not worship the image of gold that you have set up."
en.B: There are some Jews, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, whom you have put in charge of the affairs of the province of Babylon. These men pay no attention to you, O king. They do not serve your gods or worship the gold statue you have set up."
en.R: But there are some Jews, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, whom you put in charge of the province of Babylon. These men do not respect you, Your Majesty. They do not worship your gods. And they will not bow down to the gold statue you set up."

decisions.choice: Jews whom you have appointed: the charge hints at ingratitude
decisions.reason: The accusers stress that the king himself raised these foreigners to office (2:49). They make the refusal look like disloyalty to the king, not only a matter of religion.

decisions.choice: your gods: the written text may be read "your god"
decisions.reason: The consonants of the written text can be read "your god" (singular); the vowels added by the Masoretes read "your gods", as in verses 14 and 18. Either way the charge is that they will not serve the gods of Babylon.

decisions.choice: have set no regard on you: pay no attention to you
decisions.reason: The phrase means to take no notice of someone's order, to disregard it (6:14).

decisions.choice: serve ... worship (L, B, R)
decisions.reason: The first verb is "serve" in the sense of religious service to a god (verses 14, 17, 18, 28; 6:17, 21; 7:14, 27); the second is the bowing of verse 5. Readable says "worship" for the first and "bow down" for the second.

source.text: בֵּאדַ֤יִן נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר֙ בִּרְגַ֣ז וַחֲמָ֔ה אֲמַר֙ לְהַיְתָיָ֔ה לְשַׁדְרַ֥ךְ מֵישַׁ֖ךְ וַעֲבֵ֣ד נְג֑וֹ בֵּאדַ֨יִן֙ גֻּבְרַיָּ֣א אִלֵּ֔ךְ הֵיתָ֖יוּ קֳדָ֥ם מַלְכָּֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: Then Nebuchadnezzar in rage and fury said to bring Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego; then the men these were brought before the king.

en.L: Then Nebuchadnezzar, in rage and fury, ordered [them] to bring Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. Then these men were brought before the king.
en.B: Then Nebuchadnezzar, in a furious rage, ordered that Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego be brought in. So these men were brought before the king.
en.R: Nebuchadnezzar became very angry. He ordered his men to bring Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego to him. So they were brought to the king.

decisions.choice: in rage and fury: the king's anger is stressed
decisions.reason: The two words for anger stand together to show how great it was. The king's fury rises through the chapter (verse 19).

decisions.choice: in a furious rage (B)
decisions.reason: Balanced joins the two words for anger into one phrase.

source.text: עָנֵ֤ה נְבֻֽכַדְנֶצַּר֙ וְאָמַ֣ר לְה֔וֹן הַצְדָּ֕א שַׁדְרַ֥ךְ מֵישַׁ֖ךְ וַעֲבֵ֣ד נְג֑וֹ לֵֽאלָהַ֗י לָ֤א אִֽיתֵיכוֹן֙ פָּֽלְחִ֔ין וּלְצֶ֧לֶם דַּהֲבָ֛א דִּ֥י הֲקֵ֖ימֶת לָ֥א סָֽגְדִֽין׃

records.literal_gloss: Answering Nebuchadnezzar and saying to them: is it true, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, my gods you are not serving, and the image of gold which I have set up you are not paying homage?

en.L: Nebuchadnezzar answered and said to them, "Is it true, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, that you do not serve my gods, and do not worship the image of gold that I have set up?
en.B: Nebuchadnezzar said to them, "Is it true, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, that you do not serve my gods or worship the gold statue I have set up?
en.R: Nebuchadnezzar asked them, "Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, is it really true that you refuse to worship my gods? Is it true that you will not bow down to the gold statue I have set up?

decisions.choice: is it true: the question may also mean "is it on purpose"
decisions.reason: The rare word that opens the question may mean "is it true?" or "is it deliberate?" The king asks either whether the report is true or whether the three refuse on purpose.

decisions.choice: my gods ... the image I have set up
decisions.reason: The king now calls the gods "my gods" and the image "the image I have set up". Refusing them is refusing him.

decisions.choice: two questions (R)
decisions.reason: Readable splits the question in two, so that each charge is clear.

source.text: כְּעַ֞ן הֵ֧ן אִֽיתֵיכ֣וֹן עֲתִידִ֗ין דִּ֣י בְעִדָּנָ֡א דִּֽי־תִשְׁמְע֡וּן קָ֣ל קַרְנָ֣א מַשְׁרוֹקִיתָ֣א קַתְר֣וֹסשַׂבְּכָ֡א פְּסַנְתֵּרִין֩ וְסוּמְפֹּ֨נְיָ֜ה וְכֹ֣ל׀זְנֵ֣י זְמָרָ֗א תִּפְּל֣וּן וְתִסְגְּדוּן֮ לְצַלְמָ֣א דִֽי־עַבְדֵת֒ וְהֵן֙ לָ֣א תִסְגְּד֔וּן בַּהּ־שַׁעֲתָ֣ה תִתְרְמ֔וֹן לְגֽוֹא־אַתּ֥וּן נוּרָ֖א יָקִֽדְתָּ֑א וּמַן־ה֣וּא אֱלָ֔הּ דֵּ֥ייְשֵֽׁיזְבִנְכ֖וֹן מִן־יְדָֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: Now, if you are ready, that at the time that you hear [the] sound of the horn, the pipe, lyre, trigon, harp and bagpipe, and all kinds of music, you fall down and pay homage to the image which I have made, [well]; and if not you pay homage, at that moment you will be thrown into [the] midst of [the] furnace of the fire burning; and who is the god who will deliver you from my hands?

en.L: Now if you are ready, at the time you hear the sound of the horn, the pipe, the lyre, the trigon, the harp and the bagpipe, and every kind of music, to fall down and worship the image that I have made, [well and good]. But if you do not worship, at that moment you will be thrown into the midst of a furnace of burning fire; and who is the god who will deliver you out of my hands?"
en.B: Now then, if you are ready to fall down and worship the statue I have made when you hear the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe and every kind of music, very well. But if you do not worship, you will immediately be thrown into a blazing furnace. And what god is there who can rescue you from my power?"
en.R: Now I will give you another chance. When you hear the horns, flutes, lyres, zithers, harps, bagpipes and all the other instruments, bow down and worship the statue I made. If you do, all will be well. But if you do not, you will be thrown at once into a very hot furnace. Then no god will be able to save you from me!"

decisions.choice: if you are ready ...: a sentence the king leaves unfinished
decisions.reason: The king does not say what will happen if they obey; the Aramaic breaks off. The sense is "well and good", or "you will be spared". The king offers them a second chance.

decisions.choice: who is the god who will deliver you out of my hands?
decisions.reason: The king's boast echoes the Assyrian commander's words to Jerusalem: "Who among all the gods of the lands has delivered their land out of my hand?" (2 Kings 18:35; Isaiah 36:20). In both stories the God of Israel answers the challenge.

decisions.choice: [well and good] (L); very well (B)
decisions.reason: Literal supplies the words the king leaves unsaid in brackets, and Balanced gives them without (m1). Readable says "another chance" and "all will be well" to show the same.

source.text: עֲנ֗וֹ שַׁדְרַ֤ךְ מֵישַׁךְ֙ וַעֲבֵ֣ד נְג֔וֹ וְאָמְרִ֖ין לְמַלְכָּ֑א נְבֽוּכַדְנֶצַּ֔ר לָֽא־חַשְׁחִ֨ין אֲנַ֧חְנָה עַל־דְּנָ֛ה פִּתְגָ֖ם לַהֲתָבוּתָֽךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: They answered, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, and saying to the king: O Nebuchadnezzar, not needing [are] we concerning this matter to return to you an answer.

en.L: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego answered, saying to the king, "O Nebuchadnezzar, we are not in need of returning an answer to you concerning this matter.
en.B: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego replied to the king, "Nebuchadnezzar, we do not need to defend ourselves before you in this matter.
en.R: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego answered the king, "Nebuchadnezzar, we do not need to try to defend ourselves to you.

decisions.choice: to the king, O Nebuchadnezzar: they address him by name
decisions.reason: The three do not open with the court's greeting (verse 9); they speak to the king plainly, by name. Some read the name with "the king", "to King Nebuchadnezzar"; the Aramaic can be read either way, and the sense is hardly changed.

decisions.choice: we have no need to answer you: we do not need to defend ourselves
decisions.reason: They do not deny the charge or plead for mercy. Their answer is not rude but firm: there is nothing to argue, because their decision is made.

decisions.choice: defend ourselves (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "return an answer" means here (m2).

source.text: הֵ֣ן אִיתַ֗י אֱלָהַ֨נָא֙ דִּֽי־אֲנַ֣חְנָא פָֽלְחִ֔ין יָכִ֖ל לְשֵׁיזָבוּתַ֑נָא מִן־אַתּ֨וּן נוּרָ֧א יָקִֽדְתָּ֛א וּמִן־יְדָ֥ךְ מַלְכָּ֖א יְשֵׁיזִֽב׃

records.literal_gloss: If there is our God whom we serve able to deliver us from the furnace of the fire burning, and from your hand, O king, he will deliver.

en.L: If it is so, our God whom we are serving is able to deliver us from the furnace of burning fire, and out of your hand, O king, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will deliver [us].
en.B: If it comes to that, our God whom we serve is able to rescue us from the blazing furnace, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will rescue us from your power, O king.
en.R: If we are thrown into the furnace, the God we worship is able to save us from it. He will save us from your power, Your Majesty.

decisions.choice: if it is so, our God is able: their trust does not depend on the outcome
alternatives: If our God whom we serve is able to deliver us, he will deliver us
decisions.reason: The Aramaic can be read in two ways. (1) "If it is so" (if we are thrown in), "our God whom we serve is able to deliver us". (2) "If our God whom we serve exists [or: is able] to deliver us, he will deliver us." In the second reading the three are not doubting God but answering the king's challenge in verse 15 ("who is the god who will deliver you?"): if there is such a God, he will act. Either way, verse 18 shows that their decision does not depend on being rescued.

decisions.choice: able to deliver: the answer to the king's question
decisions.reason: The king asked who the god was who could deliver them (verse 15). The three take up his own word: their God is able, and will deliver.

decisions.choice: rescue (B); save (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "deliver", the king's word in verse 15; Balanced says "rescue" and Readable "save". Readable spells out "if it is so" as being thrown into the furnace (m1).

source.text: וְהֵ֣ן לָ֔א יְדִ֥יעַ לֶהֱוֵא־לָ֖ךְ מַלְכָּ֑א דִּ֤י לֵֽאלָהָךְ֙לָא־אִיתַ֣נָא פָֽלְחִ֔ין וּלְצֶ֧לֶם דַּהֲבָ֛א דִּ֥י הֲקֵ֖ימְתָּ לָ֥א נִסְגֻּֽד׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And if not, let it be known to you, O king, that your gods not [are] we serving, and to [the] image of gold which you have set up not will we pay homage.

en.L: And if not, be it known to you, O king, that your gods we are not serving, and the image of gold that you have set up we will not worship."
en.B: But even if {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} does not, you must know, O king, that we will not serve your gods, nor will we worship the gold statue you have set up."
en.R: But even if God does not save us, we want you to know, Your Majesty, that we will never worship your gods. We will never bow down to the gold statue you have set up."

decisions.choice: and if not: even if God does not rescue us
alternatives: and if he does not deliver us
and if he is not able
decisions.reason: The words most likely mean "even if God does not deliver us". Their loyalty does not depend on being rescued. On the first reading of verse 17 they may mean "and if we are not thrown in"; but most take them as the great statement of faith they have become.

decisions.choice: even if he does not (B); even if God does not save us (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "if not" means (m1).

source.text: בֵּאדַ֨יִן נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּ֜ר הִתְמְלִ֣י חֱמָ֗א וּצְלֵ֤ם אַנְפּ֨וֹהִי֙ אֶשְׁתַּנִּ֔י עַל־שַׁדְרַ֥ךְ מֵישַׁ֖ךְ וַעֲבֵ֣ד נְג֑וֹ עָנֵ֤ה וְאָמַר֙ לְמֵזֵ֣א לְאַתּוּנָ֔א חַ֨ד־שִׁבְעָ֔ה עַ֛ל דִּ֥י חֲזֵ֖ה לְמֵזְיֵֽהּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Then Nebuchadnezzar was filled [with] fury, and [the] image of his face was changed against Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego; answering and saying to heat the furnace one seven [times] over that it was proper to heat it.

en.L: Then Nebuchadnezzar was filled with fury, and the form of his face was changed against Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. He answered and ordered [them] to heat the furnace seven times more than it was usually heated.
en.B: Then Nebuchadnezzar was filled with rage, and his expression changed toward Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. He ordered the furnace heated seven times hotter than it was normally heated.
en.R: Then Nebuchadnezzar became furious with Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, and his face showed his anger. He ordered his men to make the furnace seven times hotter than usual.

decisions.choice: the image of his face was changed: his expression twisted with anger
decisions.reason: The word "image" here is the same word used for the gold image (verse 1): the king's own face changes against those who will not bow to his image.

decisions.choice: one seven: seven times, as hot as possible
decisions.reason: Seven is the number of fullness; the king orders the furnace as hot as it could be made. In his rage he does not see that a hotter fire would kill the three more quickly.

decisions.choice: his face changed (B); his face showed his anger (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "the form of his face", which echoes "image" (m1); Balanced and Readable say what it means.

source.text: וּלְגֻבְרִ֤ין גִּבָּֽרֵי־חַ֨יִל֙ דִּ֣י בְחַיְלֵ֔הּ אֲמַר֙ לְכַפָּתָ֔ה לְשַׁדְרַ֥ךְ מֵישַׁ֖ךְ וַעֲבֵ֣ד נְג֑וֹ לְמִרְמֵ֕א לְאַתּ֥וּן נוּרָ֖א יָקִֽדְתָּֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: And to men, mighty men of strength who [were] in his army, he said to bind Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, to throw [them] into the furnace of the fire burning.

en.L: And to certain mighty men of strength who [were] in his army he said to bind Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, to throw [them] into the furnace of burning fire.
en.B: He commanded some of the strongest soldiers of his army to tie up Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego and to throw them into the blazing furnace.
en.R: He told some of his strongest soldiers to tie up Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. Then they were to throw them into the very hot furnace.

decisions.choice: mighty men of strength: the strongest soldiers
decisions.reason: The phrase means the best and strongest fighting men. The king takes no chances.

decisions.choice: tie up (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "tie up" for "bind".

source.text: בֵּאדַ֜יִן גֻּבְרַיָּ֣א אִלֵּ֗ךְ כְּפִ֨תוּ֙ בְּסַרְבָּלֵיהוֹן֙ פַּטְּשֵׁיה֔וֹןוְכַרְבְּלָתְה֖וֹן וּלְבֻשֵׁיה֑וֹן וּרְמִ֕יו לְגֽוֹא־אַתּ֥וּן נוּרָ֖א יָקִֽדְתָּֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: Then the men these were bound in their trousers, their tunics, and their caps, and their garments, and were thrown into [the] midst of [the] furnace of the fire burning.

en.L: Then these men were bound in their trousers, their tunics and their caps and their [other] garments, and they were thrown into the midst of the furnace of burning fire.
en.B: So these men were tied up, still wearing their trousers, their tunics, their caps and their other clothes, and they were thrown into the blazing furnace.
en.R: So the three men were tied up in their robes, trousers, turbans and other clothes. Then the soldiers threw them into the very hot furnace.

decisions.choice: trousers, tunics, caps, garments: the clothes they wore
decisions.reason: Three of the four words are Persian and uncertain in meaning. The first may be trousers or cloaks, the second tunics or leggings, the third caps or turbans; the last is the general word for clothing. The point is that they were thrown in fully clothed, so that their unburned clothes become a sign of the miracle (verse 27).

decisions.choice: robes, trousers, turbans (R)
decisions.reason: Readable chooses familiar words from the range the Aramaic allows (m1).

source.text: כָּל־קֳבֵ֣ל דְּנָ֗ה מִן־דִּ֞י מִלַּ֤ת מַלְכָּא֙ מַחְצְפָ֔ה וְאַתּוּנָ֖א אֵזֵ֣ה יַתִּ֑ירָא גֻּבְרַיָּ֣א אִלֵּ֗ךְ דִּ֤י הַסִּ֨קוּ֙ לְשַׁדְרַ֤ךְ מֵישַׁךְ֙ וַעֲבֵ֣ד נְג֔וֹ קַטִּ֣ל הִמּ֔וֹן שְׁבִיבָ֖א דִּ֥י נוּרָֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: Because of this, since the word of the king [was] urgent and the furnace heated exceedingly, the men these who took up Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, killed them the flame of the fire.

en.L: Because the king's word was urgent and the furnace was heated exceedingly, those men who took up Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, the flame of the fire killed them.
en.B: Because the king's order was so urgent and the furnace so very hot, the flames of the fire killed the men who carried Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego up to it.
en.R: The king's order had to be obeyed at once, and the furnace was so hot that the flames killed the soldiers who carried Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego up to it.

decisions.choice: the men who took them up: the soldiers were killed by the heat
decisions.reason: "Took up" suggests that the furnace was entered from above, by a ramp or opening at the top. The heat was so great that it killed the executioners, while the three inside were unharmed (verse 27).

decisions.choice: urgent: harsh, pressing
decisions.reason: The same word as in 2:15. The king's demand for haste and heat cost his own men their lives.

decisions.choice: up to it (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "up to it" to show that the men carried them up to the furnace's opening (m1).

source.text: וְגֻבְרַיָּ֤א אִלֵּךְ֙ תְּלָ֣תֵּה֔וֹן שַׁדְרַ֥ךְ מֵישַׁ֖ךְ וַעֲבֵ֣ד נְג֑וֹ נְפַ֛לוּ לְגֽוֹא־אַתּוּן־נוּרָ֥א יָֽקִדְתָּ֖א מְכַפְּתִֽין׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And the men these, [the] three of them, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, fell into [the] midst of [the] furnace of the fire burning, bound.

en.L: And these men, the three of them, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, fell bound into the midst of the furnace of burning fire.
en.B: And these three men, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, fell, still tied up, into the blazing furnace.
en.R: And Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego fell into the very hot furnace, still tied up.

decisions.choice: the Greek additions after this verse: not part of the text
decisions.reason: The Greek versions of Daniel add sixty-eight verses after this verse: the Prayer of Azariah, prayed in the fire, a short account of the angel who drove out the flames, and the Song of the Three Young Men, a long hymn of praise. The same Greek versions also add two stories at the end of the book, or at its start: Susanna and Bel and the Dragon. None of these is in the Aramaic text translated here, and they are not translated. They are part of the Bible of the Catholic and Orthodox churches, and many Protestant Bibles print them among the Apocrypha.

decisions.choice: bound: still tied up
decisions.reason: The last word of the verse stresses that they fell in helpless. In verse 25 they are walking free.

decisions.choice: still tied up (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "still" to point forward to verse 25, where the men are loosed.

source.text: אֱדַ֨יִן֙ נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּ֣ר מַלְכָּ֔א תְּוַ֖הּ וְקָ֣ם בְּהִתְבְּהָלָ֑ה עָנֵ֨ה וְאָמַ֜ר לְהַדָּֽבְר֗וֹהִי הֲלָא֩ גֻבְרִ֨ין תְּלָתָ֜א רְמֵ֤ינָא לְגוֹא־נוּרָא֙ מְכַפְּתִ֔ין עָנַ֤יִן וְאָמְרִין֙ לְמַלְכָּ֔א יַצִּיבָ֖א מַלְכָּֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: Then Nebuchadnezzar the king was astonished, and rose in haste; answering and saying to his counselors: Not men three we threw into [the] midst of the fire bound? They answered and saying to the king: certain, O king.

en.L: Then Nebuchadnezzar the king was alarmed, and he rose in haste. He answered, saying to his counselors, "Was it not three men [that] we threw into the midst of the fire, bound?" They answered, saying to the king, "Certainly, O king."
en.B: Then King Nebuchadnezzar was amazed, and he jumped to his feet. He asked his advisers, "Did we not throw three men, tied up, into the fire?" They replied to the king, "Yes, O king, we did."
en.R: Then King Nebuchadnezzar was so surprised that he jumped up. He asked his advisers, "Did we not tie up three men and throw them into the fire?" They answered, "Yes, Your Majesty."

decisions.choice: his counselors: the king's high officials
decisions.reason: The word, used only in Daniel (3:27; 4:33; 6:8), is a title for close royal advisers.

decisions.choice: astonished: alarmed and amazed
decisions.reason: The verb means a shock of fear and surprise.

decisions.choice: tie up three men and throw them (R)
decisions.reason: Readable puts the actions in the order they happened.

source.text: עָנֵ֣ה וְאָמַ֗ר הָֽא־אֲנָ֨ה חָזֵ֜ה גֻּבְרִ֣ין אַרְבְּעָ֗ה שְׁרַ֨יִן֙ מַהְלְכִ֣ין בְּגֽוֹא־נוּרָ֔א וַחֲבָ֖ל לָא־אִיתַ֣י בְּה֑וֹן וְרֵוֵהּ֙ דִּ֣י רְֽבִיעָאָ֔ה דָּמֵ֖ה לְבַר־אֱלָהִֽין׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Answering and saying: look, I am seeing men four, loosed, walking in [the] midst of the fire, and harm there is not on them, and the appearance of the fourth [is] like a son of gods.

en.L: He answered and said, "Look! I am seeing four men, loosed, walking in the midst of the fire, and there is no harm on them; and the look of the fourth is like a son of [the] gods."
en.B: He said, "Look! I see four men, untied, walking around in the fire, and they are unharmed! And the fourth looks like a son of the gods."
en.R: He said, "Look! I see four men walking around in the fire. They are not tied up, and they are not hurt. And the fourth man looks like a heavenly being."

decisions.choice: like a son of the gods: a heavenly being, in the words of a polytheist king
decisions.reason: These are Nebuchadnezzar's words, and he speaks as a worshiper of many gods. In Aramaic, as in Hebrew, "son of the gods" means a being of the divine kind, a heavenly being, as "son of man" means a human being (compare the "sons of God" in Job 1:6; 38:7). In verse 28 the king himself calls the figure God's "angel". Many Christian readers from early times have seen in the fourth figure an appearance of the Son of God before his birth as a man, and some older Bibles printed "the Son of God" with capitals. The words of the text do not settle who the figure was; the translation gives what the king said.

decisions.choice: four men, loose, walking: three were thrown in bound, four walk free
decisions.reason: The king sees more than he expected: the bonds are gone, there are four, and the fire does them no harm. The fire has burned only their bonds (compare verse 27).

decisions.choice: a son of [the] gods (L); a son of the gods (B); a heavenly being (R); lowercase at every level
decisions.reason: The terms for Daniel set this wording. No level capitalizes the phrase or uses a divine pronoun for the figure, since these are the king's words and the text does not say more (m1). Readable says what the phrase means in Aramaic, "a heavenly being".

source.text: בֵּאדַ֜יִן קְרֵ֣ב נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּ֗ר לִתְרַע֮ אַתּ֣וּן נוּרָ֣א יָקִֽדְתָּא֒ עָנֵ֣ה וְאָמַ֗ר שַׁדְרַ֨ךְ מֵישַׁ֧ךְ וַעֲבֵד־נְג֛וֹ עַבְד֛וֹהִי דִּֽי־אֱלָהָ֥א עִלָּאָ֖ה פֻּ֣קוּ וֶאֱת֑וֹ בֵּאדַ֣יִן נָֽפְקִ֗ין שַׁדְרַ֥ךְ מֵישַׁ֛ךְ וַעֲבֵ֥ד נְג֖וֹ מִן־גּ֥וֹא נוּרָֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: Then approached Nebuchadnezzar to [the] door of [the] furnace of the fire burning; answering and saying: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, servants of God Most High, come out and come! Then were coming out Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego from [the] midst of the fire.

en.L: Then Nebuchadnezzar came near to the door of the furnace of burning fire. He answered and said, "Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, go out and come [here]!" Then Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego were coming out from the midst of the fire.
en.B: Then Nebuchadnezzar went up to the opening of the blazing furnace and called, "Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, step out and come here!" So Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego came out of the fire.
en.R: Then Nebuchadnezzar went up to the door of the very hot furnace. He shouted, "Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego! You servants of the Most High God, get out of there! Come here!" So they came out of the fire.

decisions.choice: the Most High God: a title of the God of Israel
decisions.reason: "Most High" is an old title for God as supreme over all (Genesis 14:18-20; Psalm 91:1). Nebuchadnezzar may use it as a polytheist would, of the highest god; but in Daniel it becomes the king's own confession of Israel's God (3:32; 4:14, 21-22, 31; 5:18, 21).

decisions.choice: the door of the furnace: an opening at the side
decisions.reason: The furnace seems to have had an opening at the top, where the men were thrown in (verse 22), and a door at the side through which the king could see and call to them (verse 25).

decisions.choice: the Most High God at every level
decisions.reason: The terms for Daniel set "the Most High" at every level (m1).

source.text: וּ֠מִֽתְכַּנְּשִׁין אֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנַיָּ֞א סִגְנַיָּ֣א וּפַחֲוָתָא֮ וְהַדָּבְרֵ֣י מַלְכָּא֒ חָזַ֣יִן לְגֻבְרַיָּ֣א אִלֵּ֡ךְ דִּי֩ לָֽא־שְׁלֵ֨ט נוּרָ֜א בְּגֶשְׁמְה֗וֹן וּשְׂעַ֤ר רֵֽאשְׁהוֹן֙ לָ֣א הִתְחָרַ֔ךְ וְסָרְבָּלֵיה֖וֹן לָ֣א שְׁנ֑וֹ וְרֵ֣יחַ נ֔וּר לָ֥א עֲדָ֖ת בְּהֽוֹן׃

records.literal_gloss: And gathered, the satraps, the prefects and the governors and the counselors of the king, seeing the men these, that not had the fire power over their body, and [the] hair of their head was not singed, and their trousers not were changed, and [the] smell of fire not had come on them.

en.L: And the satraps, the prefects and the governors and the king's counselors gathered, seeing these men, that the fire had had no power over their bodies; the hair of their heads was not singed, their trousers were not changed, and the smell of fire had not come upon them.
en.B: The satraps, prefects, governors and the king's advisers crowded around and saw that the fire had had no power over the bodies of these men. The hair of their heads was not singed, their trousers were not scorched, and there was no smell of fire on them.
en.R: The regional governors, the prefects, the governors and the king's advisers all crowded around them. They saw that the fire had not hurt their bodies. Not one hair on their heads was burned. Their clothes were not burned, and they did not even smell of smoke.

decisions.choice: the satraps, the prefects, the governors and the counselors: witnesses of the miracle
decisions.reason: Some of the same officials who bowed to the image (verses 2-3) now see what the God of the three has done. Each mark of fire, on body, hair, clothes and smell, is denied in turn.

decisions.choice: their trousers: the garment of verse 21
decisions.reason: The word is the first of the uncertain Persian words of verse 21. Even the clothes they were bound in are unharmed.

decisions.choice: satraps (L, B); regional governors (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 2. Readable says "clothes" for the uncertain word (m2), and "smell of smoke" for "smell of fire".

source.text: עָנֵ֨ה נְבֽוּכַדְנֶצַּ֜ר וְאָמַ֗ר בְּרִ֤יךְ אֱלָהֲהוֹן֙ דִּֽי־שַׁדְרַ֤ךְ מֵישַׁךְ֙ וַעֲבֵ֣ד נְג֔וֹ דִּֽי־שְׁלַ֤ח מַלְאֲכֵהּ֙ וְשֵׁיזִ֣ב לְעַבְד֔וֹהִי דִּ֥י הִתְרְחִ֖צוּ עֲל֑וֹהִי וּמִלַּ֤ת מַלְכָּא֙ שַׁנִּ֔יו וִיהַ֣בוּ גֶשְׁמְה֗וֹןדִּ֠י לָֽא־יִפְלְח֤וּן וְלָֽא־יִסְגְּדוּן֙ לְכָל־אֱלָ֔הּ לָהֵ֖ן לֵאלָֽהֲהֽוֹן׃

records.literal_gloss: Answering Nebuchadnezzar and saying: blessed [be] their God, of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, who has sent his angel and delivered his servants who trusted in him, and the word of the king they changed and gave their bodies that not they would serve and not pay homage to any god except their God.

en.L: Nebuchadnezzar answered and said, "Blessed be their God, the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, who sent {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} angel and rescued {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} servants, who trusted in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. They set aside the king's word and gave up their bodies, so that they would not serve or worship any god except their own God.
en.B: Nebuchadnezzar said, "Praise be to the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, who sent {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} angel and rescued {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} servants! They trusted in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, defied the king's command and were willing to give up their lives rather than serve or bow down to any god but their own.
en.R: Then Nebuchadnezzar said, "Praise the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego! He sent {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} angel to save {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} servants. They trusted {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. They disobeyed my command, and they were ready to die. They would not worship or bow down to any god except their own God.

decisions.choice: he has sent his angel: the king's account of the fourth figure
decisions.reason: The king now calls the figure of verse 25 God's angel, his messenger. God rescued his servants by sending one from his court, as he would later send his angel to shut the lions' mouths (6:23).

decisions.choice: changed the king's word and gave their bodies: defied the king's order and risked their lives
decisions.reason: To "change" the king's word is to frustrate it, to refuse to carry it out. "Gave their bodies" means that they were ready to die (compare Isaiah 50:6).

decisions.choice: blessed be their God: a pagan king praises Israel's God
decisions.reason: The king's praise anticipates the hymns of 3:31-33 and 4:31-32. As in 2:47, his words are sincere but do not yet mean that he serves this God alone.

decisions.choice: divine pronouns in the king's words
decisions.reason: Though Nebuchadnezzar speaks, "his" and "him" here refer to the God of Israel, so they take the divine pronoun setting, as Cyrus's words do in Ezra 1:2. Readable says "my command" for "the king's word", since the king is speaking of himself.

source.text: וּמִנִּי֮ שִׂ֣ים טְעֵם֒ דִּי֩ כָל־עַ֨ם אֻמָּ֜ה וְלִשָּׁ֗ן דִּֽי־יֵאמַ֤ר שָׁלוּ֙ עַ֣ל אֱלָהֲה֗וֹן דִּֽי־שַׁדְרַ֤ךְ מֵישַׁךְ֙ וַעֲבֵ֣ד נְג֔וֹא הַדָּמִ֣ין יִתְעֲבֵ֔ד וּבַיְתֵ֖הּ נְוָלִ֣י יִשְׁתַּוֵּ֑ה כָּל־קֳבֵ֗ל דִּ֣י לָ֤א אִיתַי֙ אֱלָ֣ה אָחֳרָ֔ן דִּֽי־יִכֻּ֥ל לְהַצָּלָ֖ה כִּדְנָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And from me is made a decree, that any people, nation and language which says something negligent against their God, of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, limbs will be made, and his house a refuse heap will be made, because that not there is a god another who is able to rescue like this.

en.L: And from me a decree is issued that any people, nation or language that speaks anything amiss against the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego will be made [into] limbs, and its house will be made a refuse heap, because there is no other god who is able to deliver in this way."
en.B: So I issue this decree: any people, nation or language that says anything against the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego will be torn limb from limb and their houses turned into rubbish heaps. For there is no other god who can rescue like this."
en.R: So I am giving this order: People of any nation or language who say anything against the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego will be cut to pieces, and their houses will be turned into piles of rubble. No other god can save people like this!"

decisions.choice: made into limbs ... a refuse heap: the threat of 2:5
decisions.reason: The king turns the same punishment he once threatened against his wise men (2:5) on anyone who speaks against the God of the three.

decisions.choice: something negligent: anything careless or insulting
decisions.reason: The written text has a word meaning "negligence" or "fault"; the Masoretes' reading of it means something wrong or offensive. Either way, any careless or insulting word against this God is forbidden.

decisions.choice: no other god can deliver like this
decisions.reason: The king answers his own question of verse 15 ("who is the god who will deliver you?"). His confession is that this God is unique in power, though he still speaks of "other gods".

decisions.choice: torn limb from limb ... rubbish heaps (B); cut to pieces ... piles of rubble (R)
decisions.reason: As in 2:5, Balanced and Readable say what the Aramaic threats mean.

source.text: בֵּאדַ֣יִן מַלְכָּ֗א הַצְלַ֛ח לְשַׁדְרַ֥ךְ מֵישַׁ֛ךְ וַעֲבֵ֥ד נְג֖וֹ בִּמְדִינַ֥ת בָּבֶֽל׃פ

records.literal_gloss: Then the king made prosper Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in [the] province of Babylon.

en.L: Then the king caused Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego to prosper in the province of Babylon.
en.B: Then the king gave Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego higher positions in the province of Babylon.
en.R: Then the king gave Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego even more important jobs in the province of Babylon.

decisions.choice: made them prosper: gave them success and higher rank
decisions.reason: The verb means to make prosper or succeed. The three return to their posts with greater honor.

decisions.choice: higher positions (B); even more important jobs (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "made them prosper" meant at court.

source.text: נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּ֣ר מַלְכָּ֗א לְֽכָל־עַֽמְמַיָּ֞א אֻמַיָּ֧א וְלִשָּׁנַיָּ֛א דִּֽי־דָיְרִ֥ין בְּכָל־אַרְעָ֖א שְׁלָמְכ֥וֹן יִשְׂגֵּֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: Nebuchadnezzar the king, to all the peoples, nations and languages who dwell in all the earth: your peace may it increase!

en.L: Nebuchadnezzar the king, to all the peoples, nations and languages that are dwelling in all the earth: May your peace increase!
en.B: From King Nebuchadnezzar, to all the peoples, nations and people of every language who live in all the earth: May you have abundant peace!
en.R: This letter is from King Nebuchadnezzar to people of every nation and language all over the world. I wish you peace and success!

decisions.choice: This verse is 3:31 in the Aramaic text, 4:1 in Bibles that follow the Latin and later numbering
decisions.reason: The Aramaic text ends chapter 3 with the opening of Nebuchadnezzar's letter (3:31-33) and begins chapter 4 with "I, Nebuchadnezzar". Many Bibles number these three verses 4:1-3, so their 4:1-3 is 3:31-33 here, and their 4:4-37 is 4:1-34 here. Open Word Bible follows the numbering of the text it translates. The three verses open the letter that runs through chapter 4.

decisions.choice: a royal letter: the king's greeting to his empire
decisions.reason: The verse is the opening of a letter in the form kings used: the sender, the receivers, then a greeting. The greeting "may your peace increase" is the one Darius uses in 6:26. Chapter 4 is the body of the letter, told by the king himself.

decisions.choice: the start of a hymn: verses 32-33 are a song of praise
decisions.reason: Nebuchadnezzar's greeting leads into a short song of praise (verses 32-33), like Daniel's in 2:20-23. Its last lines return at the end of the letter (4:31).

decisions.choice: the greeting as prose, the hymn in lines; peace and success (R)
decisions.reason: The terms for Daniel set 3:31-33 in lines. This verse, the letter's greeting, is a single unit in the Aramaic accents, so like a psalm title it stays on one line; the hymn of verses 32-33 is set in lines. Peace here is the full well-being of a people; Readable adds "success" to show its range. The letter is not given quotation marks, since the king himself speaks it as narrator.

source.text: אָֽתַיָּא֙ וְתִמְהַיָּ֔א דִּ֚י עֲבַ֣ד עִמִּ֔י אֱלָהָ֖א עִלָּאָ֑ה שְׁפַ֥ר קָֽדָמַ֖י לְהַחֲוָיָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: The signs and the wonders which has done with me God Most High, it seemed good before me to declare.

en.L: The signs and the wonders that the Most High God has done for me \q it has seemed good to me to declare.
en.B: I am pleased to make known to you \q the signs and wonders that the Most High God has done for me.
en.R: I want to tell you \q about the amazing things the Most High God has done for me.

decisions.choice: signs and wonders: acts of God that show his power
decisions.reason: The pair is used of God's acts in Egypt at the exodus (Deuteronomy 4:34; 6:22). Here they are what God did to Nebuchadnezzar in chapter 4: his humbling and his restoring.

decisions.choice: the Most High God: the title of 3:26
decisions.reason: The king calls Israel's God by the title he used in 3:26. In chapter 4 it becomes his main name for God (4:14, 21-22, 29, 31).

decisions.choice: I am pleased to make known (B); I want to tell you (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the main verb first, as English poetry needs, keeping two lines.

source.text: אָת֨וֹהִי֙ כְּמָ֣ה רַבְרְבִ֔ין וְתִמְה֖וֹהִי כְּמָ֣ה תַקִּיפִ֑ין מַלְכוּתֵהּ֙ מַלְכ֣וּת עָלַ֔ם וְשָׁלְטָנֵ֖הּ עִם־דָּ֥ר וְדָֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: His signs, how great! And his wonders, how mighty! His kingdom [is] a kingdom everlasting, and his dominion [is] with generation and generation.

en.L: His signs, how great [they are]! \q And {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} wonders, how mighty! \q His kingdom [is] a kingdom of all ages, \q and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} dominion [is] with generation and generation.
en.B: How great are {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} signs! \q How powerful are {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} wonders! \q His kingdom is a kingdom for all ages; \q {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} rule lasts through every generation.
en.R: His miracles are great! \q His wonders are mighty! \q His kingdom will never end. \q He will rule over people in every age.

decisions.choice: his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom: the words of Psalm 145:13
decisions.reason: The lines are close to Psalm 145:13: "Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and your dominion endures through all generations." They return at the end of the letter (4:31) and in Darius's decree (6:27), and they answer the dream of chapter 2: only God's kingdom lasts forever (2:44).

decisions.choice: with generation and generation: through all generations
decisions.reason: The Aramaic says that his rule is "with generation and generation", that is, it lasts from one generation to the next, without end.

decisions.choice: the verse set in four lines; miracles (R)
decisions.reason: The four lines follow the Aramaic accents. Inside a sentence, "his" for God takes the divine pronoun setting; at the start of a sentence it is capitalized either way. Readable says "miracles" for "signs". The last two lines reuse the published wording of Psalm 145:13 at each level, changing "your" to "his", since the Aramaic says almost the same (m1).
